source_refs.note: Chapter 13 exercise (PDF 302-304), solved: 10 MCQs keyed from the chapter (no key printed), 16 short parts (b/c and n/o joined) and 4 descriptive questions with model answers. MCQ V, Short b/c and p carry Book corrections.

blocks.text: Q.1 Four choices are given for each question. Select the correct choice.

blocks.prompt: I. Which halogen molecule has the strongest bond?
blocks.explanation: Bond energies (Table 13.3): F₂ 156, Cl₂ 243, Br₂ 193, I₂ 151 kJ mol⁻¹. Cl₂ has the highest. F₂ is weak because its small atoms bring the lone pairs close and they repel each other (13.3).

blocks.prompt: II. The volatility of the halogens (Group 17) generally _________ as you move down the group (from Fluorine to Iodine).
blocks.explanation: Down the group the molecules become larger and more polarizable, so London dispersion forces become stronger, boiling points rise and volatility decreases (13.1, 13.2).

blocks.prompt: III. Which one of the following halogen molecules has strongest oxidizing power?
blocks.explanation: Oxidizing power decreases down the group: F₂ > Cl₂ > Br₂ > I₂. F₂ has the most positive E° (+2.87 V) (13.4).

blocks.prompt: IV. The decreasing thermal stability of the halogens down the group is primarily due to the:

options.text: Decreasing bond length between the halogen atoms.
Increasing atomic radius, leading to a weaker covalent bond.
Increasing strength of van der Waals forces

blocks.explanation: Down the group the atomic radius increases, the bond becomes longer and orbital overlap poorer, so the bond is weaker and breaks more easily on heating. The chapter explains this for the hydrogen halides (HF > HCl > HBr > HI, 13.6) and for the halogen molecules from Cl₂ to I₂ (13.3).

blocks.prompt: V. Which one of the following halides has strongest reducing power?
blocks.explanation: Reducing power of halide ions: I⁻ > Br⁻ > Cl⁻ > F⁻. I⁻ is the largest ion with the lowest charge density, so it gives up its electron most easily (13.7).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The options are printed with the labels a), b), b), d): the third option, Br⁻, is printed as a second "b)". It is option (c).

blocks.prompt: VI. Which statement about the reaction between halogens and hydrogen is correct?

options.text: Iodine reacts most vigorously with hydrogen
Chlorine and hydrogen explode in darkness
Fluorine combines explosively with hydrogen even in cold and dark conditions
Bromine and hydrogen do not react at all

blocks.explanation: F₂ reacts explosively with H₂ even at low temperature and in the dark. Cl₂ needs UV light or a spark, Br₂ reacts on heating, and I₂ reacts slowly and reversibly with a catalyst (13.5).

blocks.prompt: VII. How does the acidic strength of hydrogen halides change as you move down the group?

options.text: It decreases from HF to HI.
It increases from HF to HI.

blocks.explanation: Down the group the H–X bond becomes weaker (H–F 569, H–Cl 431, H–Br 366, H–I 299 kJ mol⁻¹, Table 13.5), so H⁺ is released more easily in water: HF < HCl < HBr < HI.

blocks.prompt: VIII. Why is fluorine the most reactive halogen?

options.text: Bond length in the halogen molecule
Bond strength in the halogen molecule
Number of electrons in the halogen molecule

blocks.explanation: Reactivity of a halogen depends on its tendency to gain an electron; fluorine, the most electronegative element, has the highest tendency and forms F⁻ most readily (13.4). Its weak F–F bond (156 kJ mol⁻¹) also helps, but the main reason is its electronegativity.

blocks.prompt: IX. When aqueous silver nitrate is added to a solution containing bromide ions, a cream precipitate forms. What is the solubility of this precipitate in ammonia solution?

options.text: Partially soluble in dilute ammonia solution.
Soluble only upon heating with ammonia.

blocks.explanation: AgBr is only sparingly soluble: it does not dissolve fully in dilute ammonia (AgCl does) and dissolves in concentrated ammonia (13.8, Table 13.6). So in dilute ammonia it is partially soluble; AgI is the one that is insoluble.

blocks.prompt: X. Concentrated sulfuric acid is added to solid sodium chloride. What is the initial observation?

options.text: Steamy white fumes of hydrogen chloride are evolved.

blocks.explanation: NaCl(s) + H₂SO₄(l) → NaHSO₄ + HCl(g): steamy fumes of HCl. Cl⁻ is too weak a reducing agent to reduce H₂SO₄, so no Cl₂ forms. Brown fumes (Br₂) come from bromides and purple vapour (I₂) from iodides (13.9).

blocks.text: Q.2 Attempt the following short-answer questions:

blocks.prompt: a. Which halogen is the least reactive, which is the most? Why?
blocks.explanation:
Most reactive: fluorine; least reactive (of F, Cl, Br, I): iodine.
Reason: reactivity depends on gaining an electron. Fluorine is the smallest and most electronegative atom, with a weak F–F bond and the highest E° (+2.87 V). Iodine is the largest, least electronegative, with the lowest E° (+0.54 V).

blocks.prompt:
b. The ionic equation for a reaction is:
Br₂ + 2I⁻ →Br⁻ + I₂.
c. Explain which species is oxidized in this reaction. Why?
blocks.explanation:
I⁻ is oxidized: each iodide ion loses an electron, and its oxidation state rises from −1 to 0 in I₂ (2I⁻ → I₂ + 2e⁻).
Br₂ is reduced (0 to −1) and acts as the oxidizing agent. This happens because Br₂ is a stronger oxidizing agent than I₂ (E° +1.07 V vs +0.54 V), so bromine displaces iodine.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The equation is printed unbalanced, Br₂ + 2I⁻ → Br⁻ + I₂. One Br₂ molecule gives two bromide ions: Br₂ + 2I⁻ → 2Br⁻ + I₂.

blocks.prompt: d. What is role of London dispersion forces in the trend of volatility of halogens?
blocks.explanation: Halogens are non-polar, so only London (id-id) forces hold their molecules together. Down the group, molecules get larger and more polarizable, so these forces become stronger; more energy is needed to separate the molecules, boiling points rise and volatility decreases (F₂, Cl₂ gases; Br₂ liquid; I₂ solid).

blocks.prompt: e. How does the reactivity of halogens with hydrogen vary?
blocks.explanation:
It decreases down the group: F₂ > Cl₂ > Br₂ > I₂.
F₂ explodes with H₂ even in cold and dark; Cl₂ reacts in UV light or with a spark; Br₂ reacts on heating; I₂ reacts slowly and reversibly at high temperature with a catalyst (H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2HI).

blocks.prompt: f. Which halogen is used as an antiseptic? How does it work?
blocks.explanation:
Iodine (as tincture of iodine, a solution of iodine in alcohol) is used as an antiseptic on minor cuts (Chapter 16 lists tincture iodine as a disinfectant for cuts).
It works as an oxidizing agent: it oxidizes the proteins and enzymes of bacteria and other microbes and kills them (beyond the chapter).

blocks.prompt: g. What is the colour change when chlorine displaces bromine?
blocks.explanation:
Cl₂ + 2Br⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + Br₂
When chlorine water is added to a colourless bromide solution (e.g. KBr), the solution turns orange to reddish-brown because free bromine is formed.

blocks.prompt: h. How the halogen acids are ionized in water?
blocks.explanation:
Hydrogen halides dissolve in water and give H⁺ (H₃O⁺) and halide ions:
HX(g) + H₂O(l) → H₃O⁺(aq) + X⁻(aq)
HCl, HBr and HI ionize completely (strong acids); HF ionizes only partially (weak acid): HF + H₂O ⇌ H₃O⁺ + F⁻ (beyond the chapter).

blocks.prompt: i. Why HF is weaker acid than HCl?
blocks.explanation: The H–F bond is much stronger (569 kJ mol⁻¹) than the H–Cl bond (431 kJ mol⁻¹) because F is small and overlaps strongly with H. So HF releases H⁺ in water with difficulty and ionizes only partially, while HCl ionizes completely. (Hydrogen bonding in HF also holds the H, beyond the chapter.)

blocks.prompt: j. Describe a simple chemical test that could be used to distinguish between aqueous solutions of potassium bromide and potassium iodide. Include the reagents and expected observations.
blocks.explanation:
Silver nitrate test followed by ammonia: add a few drops of dilute HNO₃ and then aqueous AgNO₃ to each solution.
KBr: cream precipitate of AgBr, which dissolves in concentrated NH₃(aq).
KI: yellow precipitate of AgI, insoluble in both dilute and concentrated NH₃(aq).
Ag⁺ + Br⁻ → AgBr(s); Ag⁺ + I⁻ → AgI(s)

rows: Precipitate insoluble in dilute and concentrated NH₃

blocks.prompt: k. Explain the chemical principles behind the use of chlorine as a disinfectant in water purification. Include relevant chemical equations in your explanation.
blocks.explanation:
1. Chlorine hydrolyses in water: Cl₂(g) + H₂O(l) → HCl(aq) + HClO(aq)
2. Chloric(I) acid (hypochlorous acid) is a weak acid and partly dissociates: HOCl ⇌ H⁺ + OCl⁻
3. HOCl and OCl⁻ are the active species. They oxidize proteins, lipids, enzymes and nucleic acids of bacteria, which kills them.
4. HOCl is more effective because it is neutral and penetrates cell walls easily; it predominates at pH 6–7.5.

blocks.prompt: l. Describe one significant disadvantage associated with the use of chlorine in water purification.
blocks.explanation:
Chlorine reacts with organic matter in water to form chlorinated by-products (such as trihalomethanes, e.g. chloroform) that can be harmful to health with long use (beyond the chapter).
Also, chlorine gas itself is very poisonous, so its storage and dosing need great care (13.11).

blocks.prompt: m. What is disproportionation reaction? Give an example.
blocks.explanation:
A reaction in which a single element is oxidized and reduced at the same time.
Example: Cl₂(g) + 2NaOH(aq, cold) → NaCl(aq) + NaClO(aq) + H₂O(l)
Chlorine goes from 0 (Cl₂) to −1 (NaCl, reduced) and to +1 (NaClO, oxidized).

blocks.prompt:
n. Chlorine gas reacts differently with sodium hydroxide solution depending on the temperature and concentration.
o. Write balanced chemical equations for the reaction of chlorine (Cl₂) with:
i) Cold, dilute sodium hydroxide (NaOH).
ii) Hot, concentrated sodium hydroxide (NaOH).
blocks.explanation:
i) Cold, dilute NaOH:
Cl₂(g) + 2NaOH(aq) → NaCl(aq) + NaClO(aq) + H₂O(l)
(sodium chlorate(I), sodium hypochlorite)
ii) Hot, concentrated NaOH:
3Cl₂(g) + 6NaOH(aq) → 5NaCl(aq) + NaClO₃(aq) + 3H₂O(l)
(sodium chlorate(V))

blocks.prompt: p. For each reaction in question l), identify the oxidation states of chlorine in the reactant (Cl₂) and in each of the chlorine-containing products. Use these oxidation states to explain why both reactions are classified as disproportionation reactions.
blocks.explanation:
Cold NaOH: Cl₂ = 0; NaCl = −1; NaClO = +1.
Hot NaOH: Cl₂ = 0; NaCl = −1; NaClO₃ = +5.
In each reaction the same element, chlorine (0), is partly reduced (to −1) and partly oxidized (to +1 or +5) at the same time, so both are disproportionation reactions.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The question refers to "question l)", but the equations for chlorine with cold and hot sodium hydroxide are asked in part o). It means: for each reaction in part o).

blocks.prompt: Q.3 Describe and explain the relative thermal stabilities of the halogen hydrides in terms of bonds strength.
blocks.explanation:
Thermal stability of a hydrogen halide is its resistance to decomposing into H₂ and X₂ on heating. It depends on the H–X bond strength.
Order of thermal stability: HF > HCl > HBr > HI
Bond dissociation energies (Table 13.5): H–F 569, H–Cl 431, H–Br 366, H–I 299 kJ mol⁻¹.
1. HF: fluorine is small and highly electronegative; strong overlap of orbitals gives a very strong H–F bond, so HF is the most stable.
2. HCl: chlorine is larger, the H–Cl bond is longer and weaker, so HCl is less stable than HF.
3. HBr: bromine is still larger; reduced overlap gives a weaker H–Br bond.
4. HI: iodine has a very large radius; poor overlap gives the weakest H–I bond, so HI is the least stable (it decomposes on heating, e.g. a hot wire in HI gives violet iodine vapour, beyond the chapter).
Conclusion: down the group atomic radius increases, bond length increases, bond energy decreases and thermal stability decreases.

blocks.prompt: Q 4. Discuss the relative reactivity of the halogen elements as oxidizing agents. Arrange F₂, Cl₂, Br₂, I₂ in increasing order of the oxidizing power.
blocks.explanation:
Halogens act as oxidizing agents: they gain electrons and become halide ions, e.g. 2Na(s) + Cl₂(g) → 2NaCl(s).
Oxidizing power decreases down the group, because the tendency to gain an electron decreases.
1. Standard electrode potentials E°(X₂/X⁻): F₂ +2.87 V, Cl₂ +1.36 V, Br₂ +1.07 V, I₂ +0.54 V. The more positive E°, the stronger the oxidizing agent.
2. Displacement: a halogen oxidizes the halide ions below it.
F₂ + 2Cl⁻ → 2F⁻ + Cl₂ (F₂ displaces Cl⁻, Br⁻ and I⁻)
Cl₂ + 2Br⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + Br₂; Cl₂ + 2I⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + I₂
Br₂ + 2I⁻ → 2Br⁻ + I₂
Iodine cannot oxidize any halide ion.
3. Factors: a halogen with low energy of dissociation, high electron affinity and high hydration energy of its ions (and, for Br₂ and I₂, the heat of vaporization) has high oxidizing power. Fluorine has a weak F–F bond and a very small F⁻ ion with high hydration energy, so it is the strongest.
Increasing order of oxidizing power: I₂ < Br₂ < Cl₂ < F₂

blocks.prompt:
Q 5. Describe the reactions that occur when chlorine is bubbled through
(i) Cold and (ii) Hot, aqueous sodium hydroxide (NaOH).
blocks.explanation:
Both are disproportionation reactions: chlorine (0) is oxidized and reduced at the same time; the products depend on temperature.
(i) Cold, dilute NaOH:
Cl₂(g) + 2NaOH(aq) → NaCl(aq) + NaClO(aq) + H₂O(l)
Products: sodium chloride and sodium chlorate(I) (sodium hypochlorite).
Oxidation states of Cl: Cl₂ 0 → NaCl −1 (reduced) and NaClO +1 (oxidized).
(ii) Hot, concentrated NaOH:
3Cl₂(g) + 6NaOH(aq) → 5NaCl(aq) + NaClO₃(aq) + 3H₂O(l)
Products: sodium chloride and sodium chlorate(V).
Oxidation states of Cl: Cl₂ 0 → NaCl −1 (five Cl atoms reduced) and NaClO₃ +5 (one Cl atom oxidized).
On heating, the chlorate(I) first formed disproportionates further into chloride and chlorate(V) (beyond the chapter: 3ClO⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + ClO₃⁻). These reactions show how temperature controls the products.

blocks.prompt: Q.6 Discuss the reducing power of halide ions with relevant reactions. Also explain the factors affecting it.
blocks.explanation:
Reducing power of halide ions increases down the group: F⁻ < Cl⁻ < Br⁻ < I⁻ (I⁻ strongest, F⁻ weakest).
Factors:
1. Ionic size: I⁻ is the largest ion; its outer electron is far from the nucleus and is lost easily. F⁻ is very small.
2. Electronegativity: decreases from F to I, so the hold on the extra electron becomes weaker.
3. Charge density: F⁻ has high charge density, which stabilizes it; I⁻ has low charge density and donates electrons easily.
Reactions with concentrated sulfuric acid show the trend (13.9):
1. F⁻: NaF + H₂SO₄ → NaHSO₄ + HF (HF fumes only; no redox)
2. Cl⁻: NaCl + H₂SO₄ → NaHSO₄ + HCl (steamy HCl fumes only; Cl⁻ cannot reduce H₂SO₄)
3. Br⁻: NaBr + H₂SO₄ → NaHSO₄ + HBr, then 2HBr + H₂SO₄ → Br₂ + SO₂ + 2H₂O
HBr reduces H₂SO₄ (S +6) to SO₂ (S +4) and is oxidized to brown Br₂.
4. I⁻: NaI + H₂SO₄ → NaHSO₄ + HI, then 8HI + H₂SO₄ → 4I₂ + H₂S + 4H₂O
HI reduces H₂SO₄ (S +6) right down to H₂S (S −2) and gives purple I₂, so I⁻ is the strongest reducing agent.
